title: Robust Sequential Experimental Design for A/B Testing
claim: Static and sequential designs ignore how current actions shape future covariates; ours uses full history and future-aware, misspecification-robust allocation.
layout: 4 panels in 2x2 grid; shaded history regions grow across panels; geometry inset
description: A 2x2 grid compares treatment allocation designs along a timeline (1, 2, ..., N-1, N). Top-left, 'Static Design': rows of covariate boxes X (blue) and action boxes A (red) with a yellow highlight only on the current X at N-1, and an arrow from X to A. Top-right, 'Sequential Design': the yellow highlight covers all earlier X and A, so allocation uses the full history. Bottom-left, 'Ours': adds a top row of basis features Ψ(X) (purple). The yellow region extends across the history and into the future step N, which is faded, showing awareness of future covariates. Bottom-right: a light-blue parallelogram holds a right-triangle sketch labeled m(A,X), f(X)≈bᵀΨ(X) and (A,Xᵀ)θ. This sketch shows a projection decomposition into the model and the misspecification part. The eye goes first to the yellow shaded regions and the bold design labels.
caption: Graphical illustration of treatment allocation strategies under different experimental designs. Static designs are offline and depend only on current observations. Sequential designs condition treatment allocation on the observed history. In contrast, our robust sequential design accounts for how current actions affect future covariates, while remaining robust to model misspecification and finite-sample-aware.
abstract: Experimental design has emerged as a powerful approach for improving the sample efficiency of A/B testing, yet existing designs rely critically on correctly specified models. We study robust sequential experimental design under model misspecification and develop a unified framework that covers both contextual bandit and dynamic settings. Theoretically, we prove that our design bounds the worst-case mean squared error of the estimated treatment effect. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach using synthetic and real-world datasets from a leading technology company.
